candidates.topic: Cleopatra's Needle and the hidden time capsule
candidates.teaser: There's a secret box buried beneath one of the world's most famous ancient monuments — and almost nobody knows what's inside.
candidates.video_title: What's Hidden Under New York's Ancient Obelisk?
candidates.video_description: New York City's Central Park holds an ancient Egyptian obelisk — and buried beneath it is a Victorian-era time capsule. The contents will surprise you.
candidates.script: There's a 3,500-year-old Egyptian obelisk standing in Central Park, New York — and almost nobody notices it. But here's where it gets strange. When workers installed it in 1881, they buried a time capsule underneath it. Inside? A Bible, a map of New York, the complete works of Shakespeare, a US census, and weirdly — a set of coins, a deck of cards, and someone's business card. It's still sitting there right now, beneath millions of footsteps every single day. So here's the question — if you could add one thing to a time capsule for the year 4500, what would you choose?

candidates.teaser: You think you see in full color — but compared to this tiny creature, you're basically colorblind.
candidates.video_title: This Shrimp Sees Colors You Can't Even Imagine
candidates.video_description: Humans see the world through three color channels. The mantis shrimp has sixteen. Scientists are still trying to understand what that even means for their perception of reality.
candidates.script: Humans see the world through three color channels — red, green, and blue. We think that's pretty good. Then there's the mantis shrimp, a tiny crustacean hiding in shallow ocean floors, and it has sixteen color-receptor channels. Sixteen. Scientists expected it to have superhuman color discrimination, but here's the twist — it's actually worse at telling similar colors apart than we are. It doesn't blend colors like a painter. It processes each wavelength separately, like reading sixteen different signals at once. Nobody fully understands what reality even looks like through those eyes. So — do you think richer senses always mean a better experience?

candidates.topic: The Black Death may have reshaped human DNA
candidates.teaser: The deadliest plague in human history didn't just kill half of Europe — it may have permanently changed what it means to be human.
candidates.video_title: The Black Death Changed Human DNA Forever
candidates.video_description: The Black Death wiped out up to half of Europe's population in the 14th century. New research shows it may have also permanently altered the human immune system at a genetic level.
candidates.script: The Black Death killed up to half of Europe's population in just four years during the 1300s. That's tens of millions of people. But scientists recently discovered something nobody expected — it didn't just reshape society, it literally rewired human DNA. Survivors carried specific immune gene variants that protected them. Those genes got passed down. Today, those exact same variants that helped people survive the plague are now linked to a higher risk of autoimmune diseases like Crohn's disease. The plague saved your ancestors — and left a hidden cost inside your very cells. Makes you wonder: what is your body still fighting that you don't even know about?

candidates.topic: The Voyager 1 probe still sends data from interstellar space
candidates.teaser: There's a human-made object drifting beyond our solar system right now — and it's still talking to us.
candidates.video_title: We Launched Something That Left Our Solar System
candidates.video_description: Voyager 1 was launched in 1977 and is now over 24 billion kilometers from Earth — the farthest human-made object ever. And it's still transmitting data back to us.
candidates.script: In 1977, NASA launched a spacecraft the size of a small car. Today, Voyager 1 is over 24 billion kilometers from Earth — so far that its radio signal, traveling at the speed of light, still takes over 22 hours to reach us. It has crossed the edge of our solar system and entered interstellar space, a region no human-made object had ever touched before. And it's running on less power than a refrigerator light bulb. Scientists expect it to go completely dark around 2030. After that, it will drift silently through the galaxy for billions of years. What do you think will find it first?

candidates.topic: Trees in a forest share nutrients through underground fungal networks
candidates.teaser: The forest floor is hiding a secret communication network that has existed for millions of years — and trees use it to keep each other alive.
candidates.video_title: Forests Have a Secret Underground Internet
candidates.video_description: Beneath every forest lies a vast fungal network connecting tree roots. Trees use it to share sugar, water, and even chemical warning signals — scientists call it the Wood Wide Web.
candidates.script: Beneath your feet in any forest, there's an internet — and it's been running for 450 million years. Trees are connected by a vast underground web of fungi called the mycorrhizal network. Through it, trees share sugar, water, and nutrients with their neighbors. Larger trees — called mother trees — actively send extra resources to younger, weaker seedlings nearby. When a tree is under insect attack, it sends chemical warning signals through the network so neighboring trees can boost their own defenses before the insects even arrive. The forest isn't just a collection of individual trees. It's a single, communicating organism. So — does that change how you feel about cutting one down?
